paper_sections.title: Salience Network Activity in Perceptual Decisions.
Experiment 3: audio-visual asynchrony and synchrony perception task

description.value: The study examined salience-network activity and directed functional interactions between the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex and bilateral anterior insulae during four perceptual decision-making tasks with parametrically varied sensory ambiguity or difficulty.

design.value: Thirty-two participants completed four perceptual decision-making tasks during two MR scanning sessions on different days within a 7-day period. The tasks included face-house discrimination, happy-angry face discrimination, audiovisual asynchrony and synchrony perception, and random-dot-motion direction discrimination. Task difficulty was manipulated by adding sensory noise or ambiguity, and fMRI BOLD activity and behavioral performance were measured. The fMRI data were analyzed with first- and second-level GLMs and Granger-causality analysis among three salience-network ROIs.

description.value: Behavioral performance accuracy for the perceptual decisions, collected outside and inside the scanner.
Time to report the perceptual decision; RT was recorded outside the scanner only.

source_definition.value: Two noise levels: clear image category (0% noise) and noisy image category (40% noise).
Asynchrony and synchrony conditions in the audiovisual asynchrony and synchrony perception task.
Random-dot-motion stimulus conditions comprising 12% and 20% color coherence, 12% and 20% color incoherence, and the 100% condition.
Rest was included in the first-level GLM; each functional session started with 30 sec of initial rest and ended with 35 sec of final rest.
The six motion parameters were entered as nuisance covariates and regressed out of the data.

description.value: One more male participant took part in face-house discrimination and in audiovisual asynchrony and synchrony perception tasks.
Six subjects participated in behavioral experiments outside the scanner to determine the highest difficulty level with performance accuracy close to 70%.

task_description.value: Participants discriminated images of faces and houses presented with 0%, 40%, or 55% pixel-phase-randomized and Gaussian noise.

instructions.value: Participants indicated their decisions as quickly and as accurately as possible; they reported house versus face using right versus left responses.

stimuli.value: Fourteen face images and 14 house images from F.A.C.E. Training, equalized for luminance and degraded by image pixel phase randomization with addition of Gaussian noise; stimuli subtended 4.34° by 6.08° visual angles.

task_performance_measures.value: response time (RT), recorded outside the scanner

task_description.value: Participants discriminated happy and angry human face images presented as clear or noisy stimuli.

instructions.value: Participants indicated whether the face was happy or angry using left or right responses.

stimuli.value: Two sets of human face images, a happy set and an angry set, each consisting of eight images, four males and four females; images were presented with 0% or 40% noise.

task_performance_measures.value: response time (RT), recorded outside the scanner

task_name.value: audio-visual asynchrony and synchrony perception task

task_description.value: Participants judged whether paired auditory and visual stimuli were synchronous or asynchronous, with audiovisual timing varied around each participant's threshold for simultaneity.

instructions.value: Participants reported synchrony with a left response and asynchrony with a right response.

stimuli.value: A 440-Hz, 30-ms tone paired with a 30-ms yellow-red disc flash of 0.7 cm radius; the flash was presented centrally and the beep was delivered through earphones.

task_performance_measures.value: response time (RT), recorded outside the scanner

task_name.value: random dot motion (RDM) direction discrimination task

task_description.value: Participants discriminated leftward versus rightward motion in noisy random-dot fields while color coherence and color incoherence conditions varied the relationship between dot color and motion direction.

instructions.value: Participants reported leftward motion with a left response and rightward motion with a right response.

stimuli.value: Randomly moving noisy fields of red and green dots were presented within a circular aperture. Coherence levels were 12%, 20%, and 100%; dots were redrawn every 50 ms and presented for 34 ms against a black background circular aperture of 7.5 cm diameter.

task_performance_measures.value: response time (RT), recorded outside the scanner

instrument.value: 3-Tesla Siemens scanner available at the Georgia State University and Georgia Institute of Technology Center for Advanced Brain Imaging, Atlanta, Georgia

description.value: T2*-weighted gradient echo-planar imaging protocol with TE=30 msec, TR=2000 msec, flip angle=90°, voxel size=3×3×3 mm3, field of view=204×204 mm, matrix size=68×68, and 37 axial slices each of 3 mm thickness. Face-house runs were 614 sec each, and happy-angry face runs were 674 sec each; audiovisual and RDM run durations were not stated.

High-resolution anatomical images were acquired for anatomical references using a magnetization-prepared rapid gradient-echo sequence with TR=2250 msec, TE=4.18 msec, flip angle=9°, inversion time=900 msec, and voxel size=1×1×1 mm3.

MRI data preprocessing included slice timing correction, motion correction, coregistration to the individual anatomical image, normalization to the Montreal Neurological Institute template, and spatial smoothing.

software.value: Statistical Parametric Mapping (SPM8; Wellcome Trust Center, London)

steps.value: normalization to Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) template
spatial smoothing of the normalized image with an 8-mm isotropic Gaussian kernel

model_settings.value: A separate GLM was specified for each participant according to task sequences and behavioral responses. Only correct trials for each condition, rest, and six motion parameters were included; the motion parameters were entered as nuisance covariates and regressed out.

Individual contrast images resulting from the first-level analysis were entered into a second-level analysis for a separate one-sample t-test. Statistical maps were thresholded at p<0.05 familywise error correction with cluster extent k≥10, except for the moving-dot task, which used p<0.01 FWE correction.

BOLD time series from three 6-mm-radius ROIs were hemodynamically deconvolved. The optimal autoregressive model order was selected by comparing nonparametric and parametric power spectra. Time-domain Granger causality values were obtained by integrating causality spectra over the full frequency range. Significance thresholds were based on at least 1000 random permutations, maximum GC values per permutation, gamma-distribution fitting, and p<10−3; conditional GC was used to rule out mediated interactions.

estimator.value: parametric spectral Granger causality with permutation testing and conditional Granger causality
